name: Depth Study
subtitle: Your music, your project
blurb: The last unit of Year 10, and the one you choose. You pick an area of music you care about, plan a project in performing, composing or listening, build it across Term 4, and present it to the class.
outcomes: performs repertoire with stylistic awareness and musical expression
manipulates and combines the elements of music in performance to communicate musical ideas
improvises, arranges or composes with stylistic understanding and musical expression
manipulates and combines the elements of music to create musical ideas
uses listening skills to analyse music in relation to stylistic, cultural, historical and social contexts
uses listening skills to evaluate how the elements of music are manipulated and combined

assessment.name: AT4 Depth Study
assessment.detail: Your final product, presented in class. 20 marks, worth 25%. You are marked on what you make and how you present it, using the rubric for the focus area you chose. There is no written report.
assessment.note: The task notification is in Canvas. Your outcomes depend on the focus area you choose.

milestones.detail: Look through the idea bank and decide whether you are performing, composing, investigating, or combining two of them.
Your proposal is signed off, so you can start work in the first week back.

milestones.what: Plan set and success criteria agreed
milestones.detail: Your week-by-week plan to the due date is written, and the class has worked out together what a good project looks like.
You share where you are up to and get one strength and one next step from your feedback partner.
You mark your own work against the success criteria, find the gaps, and agree your final priorities.
Hand in your product and present it to the class, with a short spoken introduction.
The rest of the presentations, and a look back at what you made.

weeks.label: Before Term 4
weeks.title: Choosing and proposing
weeks.intro: The work that decides how the whole unit goes. You choose a project that you actually care about and can actually finish, then write the plan that gets it approved.

lessons.where: worked on in Term 3, Weeks 9 and 10
lessons.title: Choose your project
lessons.intention: I can choose a depth study project I care about and can finish in the time I have.
criteria: I can name my focus area: performing, composing, listening, or a combination
I can say what I will make or present
I can explain why this project is the right size for eight to ten hours of class time

blocks.text: A self-directed music investigation in an area of personal interest. You choose the area, you choose the product, and you drive the work. This is the most independent unit of Year 10.

blocks.title: What you could do
blocks.lead: Three focus areas, and a fourth option that combines two of them. Each row is the same project at three sizes, so find the one that matches where you actually are. You can also propose your own idea, as long as it fits a focus area.

focuses.name: Performing
focuses.product: a live or recorded performance, plus program notes or a rehearsal log.
tiers: Entry
Prepare and perform one piece on your instrument, with short program notes.
Core
Perform a set of two or three linked pieces, or record a multitrack cover of a song you love.
Extension
Lead a small ensemble, or perform a demanding programme you have chosen and rehearsed yourself.

focuses.name: Composing
focuses.product: a recording or demo, plus a score or lead sheet if your piece has one, and a short rationale.
tiers: Entry
Write a short original piece or song section and explain the choices you made.
Core
Write an original song and record a demo, or arrange an existing song in a new style.
Extension
Compose to a brief: music for a film scene, a game, an artwork, or a produced track.

focuses.name: Listening and Investigation
focuses.product: a multimodal presentation or a viva voce, with musical examples you play.
tiers: Entry
A short presentation analysing how the elements are used in a track you already love.
Core
A multimodal investigation of an artist, a genre or a soundtrack, with examples.
Extension
A viva voce where you argue a case about a style and answer questions on it.

focuses.name: Combination
focuses.product: a product from each area you choose, plus a short piece of writing linking them.
tiers: Entry
Compose a short piece and then perform it yourself.
Core
Investigate a style, then perform or compose something in it.
Extension
Research, compose and perform, and explain how each part fed the next.

blocks.title: How to choose well
items: Interest. Pick something you actually care about. You are going to live with this for a term, and it shows in the final product when you do not.
Skill. Pick something you can already do most of, and stretch the last part. A project that needs a skill you have not started learning is a project you will not finish.
Time. You have eight to ten hours of class time and the weeks between. Halve your first idea if it does not fit that, and do the smaller thing properly.

blocks.text: Write down two projects you would genuinely like to do, one from each of two different focus areas. For each one, note what you would hand in and the single hardest part. Bring both to your proposal conference: choosing between two real options is much easier than inventing one on the spot.
In one sentence: what do you want to make, and why that one?

lessons.where: worked on in Term 3, Week 10 and Term 4, Week 1
lessons.title: Write your proposal
lessons.intention: I can write a proposal that sets out my goal, my product, my plan and how I will know it worked.
criteria: My goal or focus question says what I am trying to do, make or find out
My product is something specific I can hand in
My plan has a milestone for each week up to the due date
My success criteria describe what a good version of my project looks like

blocks.title: What a proposal has to do
items: Make the project real. A goal like "do something with jazz" cannot be started on Monday. "Learn and record two Miles Davis heads with a backing track" can.
Make it checkable. If nobody can tell whether you have finished, you cannot tell either.
Make it small enough. Your plan has to fit the weeks that actually exist, including the ones where you are away or something breaks.

blocks.title: Your proposal
blocks.prompt: Fill this in on screen, then talk it through with Mr Edwards to get it approved. What you type stays on this device, so finish it in one sitting or write it up somewhere safe.

rows.label: Focus area
rows.prompt: Performing, Composing, Listening and Investigation, or a combination?

rows.label: My goal
rows.prompt: What are you trying to do, make or find out? Write it so someone else could tell when you had done it.

rows.label: My product
rows.prompt: What exactly will you hand in or present? Name the thing: a recording, a demo and lead sheet, a viva voce, a multimodal presentation.

rows.label: My outcomes
rows.prompt: Which outcomes will your project give evidence for? They come from the focus area you chose, and they are listed on the unit page.

rows.label: My plan
rows.prompt: What will you have done by the end of each week, up to the due date in Week 4? Give each week one milestone you could tick off.

rows.label: What I need
rows.prompt: Instruments, software, recording gear, a practice room, and the parts where you will need help.

rows.label: Success criteria
rows.prompt: How will you know your project worked? Write three things a good version of it would have. We build these together from the marking guide.

blocks.text: The agreed signs that show your project has met the standard. They are not the same as finishing it. A project can be handed in complete and still miss what it was aiming at, which is exactly what these are for.
Swap proposals with someone doing a different focus area. Read theirs and ask one question about the part you could not picture. The parts nobody can picture are the parts that go wrong in Week 3.
Which week of your plan is the one most likely to slip, and what will you do about it?

weeks.label: Term 4, Weeks 1 to 3
weeks.title: Developing it
weeks.intro: The longest stretch of the unit. You build your product, get feedback twice, and keep a running record of your thinking so the write-up for your presentation is easy at the end.

lessons.where: worked on across Term 4, Weeks 1 to 3
lessons.title: Develop it
lessons.intention: I can work steadily on my project, use feedback to improve it, and keep a process journal that shows my thinking.
criteria: I can show what I have done against my plan at each progress check
I can give a classmate one strength and one next step, and use feedback I am given
I can keep a process journal that records what I did, what I changed, and why

blocks.text: A short, regular record of your project as you make it: what you worked on, what you changed and why, and what you will do next. It is not a diary of feelings, it is evidence of your thinking, and it is what makes your spoken introduction easy to write later.

blocks.title: What a good journal entry has
items: What you actually did this session, in one line.
One decision you made and the reason for it. "I changed the key because..." is worth more than "I worked on the chorus."
One thing you will do next session, so you do not lose ten minutes remembering where you were.

blocks.title: Journal entry
blocks.prompt: Fill this in at the end of a work session. It only holds one entry at a time, so copy it somewhere safe (a notes app, a photo, your workbook) before you clear it and write the next one.

rows.label: Date and session
rows.prompt: Which lesson or session is this?

rows.label: What I worked on
rows.prompt: What did you actually do this session?

rows.label: What I changed and why
rows.prompt: Any decision you made and the reason for it.

rows.label: What's next
rows.prompt: What will you do in your next session?

blocks.title: Peer feedback
blocks.prompt: Use this with your feedback partner at each progress check (Term 4, Week 2 and Week 3). Swap roles: fill it in for their project, then have them fill it in for yours.

rows.label: Whose project
rows.prompt: Who are you giving feedback to?

rows.label: What I saw or heard
rows.prompt: Describe what they showed you, without judging it yet.

rows.label: One strength
rows.prompt: What is working well?

rows.label: One next step
rows.prompt: What is the single most useful thing they could do next?

blocks.text: One sentence: what did this progress check tell you to change?

weeks.label: Term 4, Weeks 3 to 4
weeks.title: Refining and finalising
weeks.intro: You compare your work honestly against the rubric for your focus area, fix the highest-impact gaps first, and check your submission is actually ready before the due date.

lessons.where: worked on in Term 4, Weeks 3 and 4
lessons.title: Refine and finalise
lessons.intention: I can check my project against the rubric for my focus area, fix the gaps that matter most, and get it ready to submit.
criteria: I can compare my work honestly against the rubric for my focus area
I can pick the highest-impact fix for the time I have left
I can check my submission is complete before the due date

blocks.title: How to self-assess without kidding yourself
items: Read all five bands for a criterion before you decide where you sit, not just the top one. The middle bands describe most real projects.
Be specific. "I'm okay at technique" is not a self-assessment; "my technique is secure in the first half but breaks down in the fast section" is.
Fix the biggest gap first. A perfect ending on a project that is not finished scores worse than a finished project with a rough ending.

blocks.title: Performing rubric
blocks.lead: Four criteria, 5 marks each, 20 marks total. Use this if your focus area is Performing.

criteria.name: Technical control and accuracy
bands: Highly developed, fluent and secure technique throughout; negligible errors.
Strong control; mostly fluent with minor inconsistencies.
Sound control; generally accurate with some errors.
Limited control; frequent errors affect the performance.

criteria.name: Expression and stylistic interpretation
bands: Sophisticated, consistent expression and stylistic understanding.
Effective expression and mostly appropriate style.
Some expression and stylistic awareness; inconsistent.
Little or no expression or stylistic awareness.

criteria.name: Realisation of intention and repertoire choice
bands: Ambitious, well-chosen program fully realised as intended.

criteria.name: Presentation and communication
bands: Confident, engaging presentation with a clear spoken introduction.

blocks.title: Composing rubric
blocks.lead: Four criteria, 5 marks each, 20 marks total. Use this if your focus area is Composing.

criteria.name: Manipulation and combination of the elements of music
bands: Manipulates and combines elements with control and imagination throughout.
Manipulates and combines several elements effectively.
Uses some elements with limited combination.
Uses few elements with little control.

criteria.name: Stylistic understanding and musical expression
bands: Strong, consistent style and expressive intent.
Clear style and expression with minor lapses.

criteria.name: Structure, development and realisation of intention
bands: Well-structured, developed work that fully realises the concept.
Clear structure and development; concept realised.

criteria.name: Presentation and communication (demo and spoken introduction)
bands: Polished recording or demo with a clear spoken introduction.

blocks.title: Listening and Investigation rubric
blocks.lead: Four criteria, 5 marks each, 20 marks total. Use this if your focus area is Listening and Investigation.

criteria.name: Analysis of how the elements of music are used
bands: Precise, insightful analysis of how elements are manipulated and combined.
Clear analysis of several elements and how they combine.

criteria.name: Understanding of style and context
bands: Thorough understanding of stylistic, cultural, historical or social context.
Good understanding of context with relevant links.

criteria.name: Musical evidence and terminology
bands: Uses precise terminology and well-chosen musical examples throughout.
Uses correct terminology and relevant examples.
Some terminology and examples; not always accurate.

criteria.name: Presentation and communication (multimodal or viva voce)
bands: Clear, well-structured, engaging presentation with confident delivery.

blocks.title: Self-assessment against the rubric
blocks.prompt: Find the rubric for your focus area above. For each of the four criteria, decide honestly which band you are closest to right now.

rows.label: My focus area
rows.prompt: Performing, Composing, or Listening and Investigation?

rows.label: Where I am strong
rows.prompt: Which criterion and band are you closest to at the top end?

rows.label: Where I need to improve most
rows.prompt: Which criterion and band are you weakest in, and what would move it up a band?

rows.label: My plan for the time I have left
rows.prompt: What will you actually do in your remaining sessions?

blocks.title: Before you submit
items: Your product is uploaded to the correct Canvas assignment, or handed to Mr Edwards, by the due date.
Any score, lead sheet, or slides that are part of your product are included, not left on your device.
Instruments, equipment, backing tracks or files you need for your presentation are ready to bring.
If you used generative AI for planning or research, you have noted what you used it for. It has no place in composing, arranging, producing, performing, or writing your spoken introduction.

blocks.text: What is the one thing that would improve your project the most before you submit?

weeks.label: Term 4, Weeks 4 to 5
weeks.title: Presenting it
weeks.intro: You submit your product, present it to the class with a short spoken introduction, and then take your turn as an audience member for everyone else's presentations.

lessons.where: worked on in Term 4, Weeks 4 and 5
lessons.title: Present it
lessons.intention: I can introduce my project to the class, present it clearly, and give useful feedback as an audience member.
criteria: I can write a short spoken introduction that sets up what I made and why
I can present my product clearly in the time I have
I can give a classmate useful feedback on their presentation

blocks.text: A short, unscripted-sounding explanation you give before your performance, recording, or investigation starts. It tells the class what you set out to do, so they know what to listen or watch for. It is part of your mark, not a formality before the real thing starts.

blocks.title: What a good spoken introduction covers
items: What you made. One sentence naming your product: the piece, the song, the investigation topic.
Why you chose it. The genuine reason, even if it is simple. "I wanted to get better at improvising" is a real reason.
What to listen or watch for. Point the class at the one thing you are proudest of, so they notice it.

blocks.title: Plan your spoken introduction
blocks.prompt: Draft it here, then practise saying it out loud until it sounds like you talking, not you reading.

rows.label: What I made
rows.prompt: One sentence.

rows.label: Why I chose it
rows.prompt: The real reason.

rows.label: What to listen or watch for
rows.prompt: The one thing you want the class to notice.

blocks.title: Audience feedback
blocks.prompt: Fill this in while you watch a classmate present, then hand or tell them your two lines afterwards. Clear it and reuse it for the next presentation.

rows.label: Who presented
rows.prompt: Whose project did you watch?

rows.label: What I noticed
rows.prompt: What stood out about what they made or how they presented it?

rows.label: One thing I'd ask them
rows.prompt: A genuine question you'd want to know the answer to.

blocks.text: After watching the showcase, what is one thing you would try in your own next project?
